title: Switch expressions and patterns
body: Pattern matching tests a value's shape and extracts parts of it. Patterns appear after `is` and in `switch` expressions: `shape switch { Circle c => ..., Rect { Width: 0 } => ..., _ => ... }`. A switch expression yields a value; arms are tried top to bottom and the first match wins.

Common patterns: type patterns (`Circle c`), constant patterns (`0`, `null`, `"admin"`), relational patterns (`< 0`, `>= 90`), logical combinators (`and`, `or`, `not`), property patterns (`{ Status: "open", Total: > 100 }`), positional patterns for deconstructable types (`Point(0, var y)`) and the discard `_`.

`var` patterns always match and capture the value. Parenthesized and nested patterns compose: `{ Address.City: "Paris" }` uses an extended property pattern. `is not null` is the idiomatic null check because it cannot be changed by an overloaded `==`.

The compiler checks switch expressions for exhaustiveness and warns (CS8509) when some input could match no arm; at runtime such an input throws `SwitchExpressionException`. It also rejects arms that can never be reached because an earlier arm subsumes them (CS8510).
Order arms from most to least specific and avoid `_` when you want the compiler to tell you about a new case. Check for null explicitly: a type pattern never matches null.

challenge: Write a switch expression that classifies a (int Hour, bool Weekend) tuple as "sleep" (hour < 7), "brunch" (weekend and 7-11), "work" (weekday 9-16) or "free".
question: What happens at runtime when no arm of a switch expression matches?
reasoning: The compiler warns about non-exhaustive switches (CS8509); add arms or a discard to handle every input.
